title: The peacemakers (Matthew 5:9)
hook: peacemakers, not peacekeepers: they make peace where there wasn't any
carry: make peace, not just keep it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pure in heart, and your line was a single heart sees. What did you give your whole heart to? Day two hundred thirty-nine.

Every family has a peacekeeper. The one who changes the subject when politics comes up at dinner. Who says, let's not get into it. Who smooths things over so nobody storms out. It's a real gift, and often an exhausting one. But notice: under a kept peace, the problem is usually still there. The two brothers still aren't speaking. The old hurt is still sitting in the corner. The seventh line of the sermon doesn't bless the peacekeepers. It uses a different word.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY HAS A PEACEKEEPER.` → `LET'S NOT GET INTO IT.` → `A DIFFERENT WORD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The Greek word is eirenopoioi. Eirene is peace; poieo is to make, to build, the root of our word poem. Peace-makers. People who build a peace that wasn't there before. It's the only time this word appears in the whole New Testament. And the peace behind it is the Hebrew shalom. Shalom isn't just no fighting. It's wholeness: everything in its right place, nothing missing, nothing broken. So a peacemaker doesn't just stop the shouting. They go into the broken place and help build something whole. That's harder. It usually means naming what's wrong, listening to both sides, and taking some heat. Peacemakers often get shot at from both directions. Now think about the world Jesus said this in. Rome boasted of the Pax Romana, the Roman peace, a peace kept by legions and crosses. Jesus blesses a different kind: peace that's made, not enforced. And the promise: they shall be called the children of God. In Hebrew idiom, the son of something shares its character. Peacemakers are called God's children because they're doing what, Christians say, God does: making peace between people who were apart. Paul would later put the practical version this way: "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men." If it be possible. As much as lieth in you. It takes two to make peace. But you can do your half.
screen: `EIRENE PLUS POIEO: PEACE-BUILDERS.` · `SHALOM: NOTHING MISSING, NOTHING BROKEN.` · `NOT ENFORCED, BUT MADE.` · `CALLED THE CHILDREN OF GOD.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one peace today. Settle, and breathe. Think of a relationship where there's a quiet cold war: not a battle, just a chill. Someone you avoid. Something unsaid. Picture that person. Then ask: what would be my half of making peace? Maybe it's an apology. Maybe it's asking, are we okay? Maybe it's just a friendly message after a long silence. Choose the smallest real step. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for courage. The bell holds the time.
The peacemakers. Eirenopoioi, peace builders: people who make shalom where there wasn't any, and are called the children of God.
Your line: make peace, not just keep it. Today, take the smallest real step toward one peace: one message, one question, one apology. Your half is enough. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Many churches share the peace in worship, turning to neighbors to say peace be with you, and Christians, especially in the historic peace churches, work at mediation and reconciliation between people and communities.

fork.setup: at a family dinner, two relatives haven't spoken in a year. what does a peacemaker, not a peacekeeper, do?
options: change the subject so nobody fights.
quietly help them start to talk and mend it.
take one side to end it faster.
fork.reveal: peacemakers build peace where there wasn't any. keeping the peace smooths things over; making it helps mend what's broken.

original.note: Greek: peacemakers. eirene, peace, and poieo, to make. found only in Matthew 5:9 in the New Testament.

trapdoor: what you thought: peacemakers are nice people who avoid fights.
what it means: peace builders, who make shalom where there wasn't any.
what a scholar hears: eirenopoios appears only here in the New Testament; its verb comes once, in Colossians 1:20, of God making peace.

notes: eirenopoios occurs only at Matthew 5:9 in the NT (the verb eirenopoieo at Colossians 1:20). Confirm.
Colossians 1:20 uses the verb eirenopoieo (KJV: having made peace). Confirm.
'Son of' idiom meaning 'sharing the character of': standard; confirm.
Historic peace churches (Mennonite, Quaker, Church of the Brethren) mentioned in howItsDone without ranking.
